title: Life for postwar migrants

draft.title: Life for postwar migrants
card: Many postwar migrants first stayed in migrant reception centres. Bonegilla, near Albury-Wodonga in Victoria, was the largest. It opened in 1947 and housed many thousands of newcomers.
Conditions in the camps were often basic. People lived in huts, shared rooms and bathrooms, and ate in large mess halls. Some camps were hot in summer and cold in winter.

Many migrants had agreed to work where the government sent them for about two years. Some worked on big projects such as the Snowy Mountains Scheme in New South Wales, which built dams, tunnels and power stations for hydro-electricity and irrigation.
Migrants could face prejudice. Some were called names, and some had trouble getting jobs that matched their skills. Many still settled, built communities and changed Australian life.
draft.remember: Many postwar migrants began in camps and hard work, and some met prejudice, but they settled and shaped Australia.

opts: A migrant reception centre where newcomers first stayed
A dam built by migrants in the Snowy Mountains
A ship that carried assisted British migrants
A prison camp for people seen as a danger
a.why: Bonegilla was the largest migrant reception centre, where many new arrivals lived first. The Snowy Mountains Scheme was a separate project that employed many migrants, so it is not the same thing.
a.clue: Think about where migrants lived when they first arrived.

b.q: Marta arrives from Europe in 1950 and agrees to work where the government sends her. She is placed on a large hydro-electric project in the mountains. Which project is this most likely to be?
opts: The Snowy Mountains Scheme
Bonegilla migrant reception centre
The White Australia policy
The Vietnam War refugee program
b.why: The Snowy Mountains Scheme built dams, tunnels and power stations, and many migrants worked on it. Bonegilla is a tempting answer because migrants lived there, but it was a reception centre, not a work project.
b.clue: Which option was a building project for hydro-electricity?

a.best: A migrant reception centre where newcomers first stayed

problems.detail: The stem says the project is 'in the mountains', which matches the name 'Snowy Mountains Scheme'. Also, no other option is a building project (two are a policy and a program from other points, one is a reception centre). A student can pick the answer from the wording alone. The clue makes this worse by asking which option was a building project.

The scenario places a woman, Marta, as a worker on the Snowy Mountains Scheme. The Scheme's workforce was overwhelmingly male. Women displaced persons on two-year contracts were mostly sent to domestic, hospital or factory work, so this example could mislead students about who did this work. A male name, or a less specific role, would avoid this.

check.summary: The card and question a are accurate. Question b gives its answer away: 'in the mountains' matches 'Snowy Mountains', and it is the only option that is a project. Its scenario also puts a woman on the mostly male Snowy Mountains workforce.

card: Many postwar migrants first stayed in migrant reception centres. Bonegilla, near Albury-Wodonga in Victoria, was the largest. It opened in 1947 and housed many thousands of newcomers.
Conditions in the camps were often basic. People lived in huts, shared rooms and bathrooms, and ate in large mess halls. Some camps were hot in summer and cold in winter.

Many migrants had agreed to work where the government sent them for about two years. Many men worked on big projects such as the Snowy Mountains Scheme in New South Wales, which built dams, tunnels and power stations. Many women were sent to hospitals, homes or factories.

b.q: In 1952, Josef, a trained doctor from Latvia, has finished his work contract. He can only find work as a factory hand, and some workmates mock his accent. What part of the migrant experience does this show?
opts: Prejudice, such as name-calling and skills not being used
Basic conditions, such as shared huts and mess halls
A two-year agreement to work where the government chose
Big projects, such as dams built for hydro-electricity
b.why: Josef is mocked and cannot get work that matches his training, which are both forms of prejudice migrants could face. The two-year agreement is tempting, but his contract has ended, so he is no longer being sent to a job by the government.
b.clue: Look at what happens after his contract is over.
